query: For eutectic high-entropy alloys intended for structural applications, what single intervention could simultaneously increase strength and ductility? Formulate one testable hypothesis specifying the intervention, its proposed mechanism, the expected improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, the conditions under which it should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment that could falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a specific thermo-mechanical processing route (severe cold rolling followed by optimized annealing) to an as‐cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (such as AlCoCrFeNi2.1) will refine its lamellar dual-phase microstructure. This refined structure will enhance the two-hierarchical constraint effect and promote self-arrest of microcrack propagation, thereby simultaneously increasing both strength and ductility relative to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1) with a coarser lamellar dual-phase (FCC/BCC or FCC/B2) microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform severe cold rolling (or an equivalent intense plastic deformation step) followed by a controlled annealing treatment at an optimized temperature (e.g., in the range of 600–700 °C) to induce ultrafine grain refinement of the lamellar phases.
generation.conditions: The alloy must be processed under conditions that preserve the eutectic chemistry (i.e., no significant compositional segregation) and avoid excessive grain coarsening. The processing schedule should balance the degree of deformation and annealing time/temperature to achieve an ultrafine duplex microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined eutectic lamellar dual-phase microstructure with well-defined phase boundaries and a hierarchical grain structure.
generation.mechanism: The processing-induced ultrafine lamellar structure enhances the two-hierarchical constraint effect by providing a strong interface between the soft (e.g., FCC or L12) phase and hard (e.g., BCC or B2) phase. This improved constraint facilitates simultaneous strengthening (by hindering dislocation motion) and ductility (through controlled plasticity and microcrack-arresting at the interfaces).
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast state, the processed alloy is expected to exhibit a significant increase in tensile strength (potentially approaching or exceeding 1.2–1.5 GPa) while retaining or even improving ductility (with elongation values remaining above 10–14%).
generation.baseline: The as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy microstructure without post-casting thermo-mechanical processing.
generation.boundary: This effect is expected to hold in eutectic high-entropy alloys that naturally form a dual-phase lamellar structure. The benefits might be limited if processing parameters over-refine or damage the lamellar interface, or if applied to alloys that do not possess a precast eutectic architecture.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal processing parameters (amount of deformation, annealing temperature, and time) remain to be fully determined. Additionally, scale-up effects and uniformity of the refined microstructure may introduce variability in the final mechanical properties.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloy samples (e.g., AlCoCrFeNi2.1). One set will remain in the as-cast condition (baseline), and the other will undergo severe cold rolling (with a defined number of passes) followed by annealing at a specified temperature for a fixed duration. Characterize the microstructure using electron microscopy (SEM/TEM) to verify the refinement of the lamellar dual-phase structure. Then, perform tensile tests under identical conditions on both sets.
measurements: Grain size and lamellar spacing via microstructural analysis
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermo-mechanically processed samples do not show a statistically significant simultaneous improvement in both tensile strength and ductility compared to the as-cast baseline, or if the refined lamellar microstructure is not reliably achieved, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Realizing improved strength–ductility synergy in eutectic alloys acting as in situ composite materials remains a challenge in conventional eutectic systems, which is why eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs), a newly-emerging multi-principal-element eutectic category, may offer wider in situ composite possibilities. Here, we use an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA to engineer an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure that deliberately inherits its composite lamellar nature by tailored thermo-mechanical processing to achieve property combinations which are not accessible to previously-reported reinforcement methodologies. The as-prepared samples exhibit hierarchically-structural heterogeneity due to phase decomposition, and the improved mechanical response during deformation is attributed to both a two-hierarchical constraint effect and a self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanism. This work provides a pathway for strengthening eutectic alloys and widens the design toolbox for high-performance materials based upon EHEAs. To tackle the aforementioned problems, eutectic HEAs (EHEAs) [] were proposed. On the one hand, EHEAs should have the general character of traditional eutectic alloys. In this sense, EHEAs should have better fluidity and thus better castability and less casting defects [,]. On the other hand, EHEAs as one kind of in-situ composites with lamellar or rod-like eutectic microstructures might reach the balance between strength and ductility via mixing the soft FCC phase with the hard BCC phase or intermetallic compound [,,,,,,,,]. Some EHEAs indeed have outstanding properties. Lu et al. [] reported the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with simultaneous high strength (944 MPa) and good ductility (25.6%). The excellent mechanical properties do not depend significantly on derivation of eutectic compositions []. After cold-rolling and annealing, its strength reached up to 1.2 GPa and its elongation could remain at about 12% []. After cryo-rolling and annealing, its strength could reach up to 1.47 GPa while its ductility could even increase to 14% []. He et al.
